title: Unanswered prayer (2 Corinthians 12:7–9)
hook: Paul asked three times for a thorn to be removed, and it wasn't

segments.voice: Yesterday, the silence of God: Psalm twenty-two begins thou hearest not and turns to he heard. Your line was silence is not absence. Where did you let a pause stay a pause? Day one thousand three hundred eighty-nine.

Paul, writing to the church in Corinth, admits he has something wrong with him. He doesn't say what. He calls it a thorn in the flesh. And he prayed for it to go. "For this thing I besought the Lord thrice, that it might depart from me." Thrice. Three times he asked, and three times, as far as we can tell, the thorn stayed exactly where it was. The apostle writing this letter had a prayer that didn't get the answer he asked for. Today: unanswered prayer.

First, the thorn itself. Paul calls it "a thorn in the flesh, the messenger of Satan to buffet me." He never names it. Some readers guess an illness, or trouble with his eyes. Others think it was a person, an opponent who kept dogging his work. Others think it was a temptation. Because Paul leaves it unnamed, some readers set their own thorn in that space. Second, the answer. It's not silence, and it's not yes. "And he said unto me, My grace is sufficient for thee: for my strength is made perfect in weakness." The thorn stays. What's promised instead is grace, enough of it, for living with the thing that didn't go away. Some Christians say every prayer gets an answer, and sometimes the answer is no. Paul's story has a second half: no, and here is what will carry you. Third, he isn't the only one who asked three times. In the garden of Gethsemane, Jesus prays, "O my Father, if it be possible, let this cup pass from me: nevertheless not as I will, but as thou wilt." Matthew says he goes back and prays a third time, saying the same words. And the cup doesn't pass. Paul's thorn and Jesus's cup sit side by side: real requests, honestly made, and a road that went on anyway. Last, notice that Paul didn't stop asking after the first time. Three tries before he heard the answer. Unanswered prayer, in this text, is not prayer that failed. It's prayer that was heard, and answered with something other than what was asked. My grace is sufficient.

Here's the practice: pray about a thorn. Settle, and breathe. Name one thing that's stayed with you no matter how much you've wanted it gone: a health problem, a hard relationship, a habit, a loss. Don't try to solve it. Just let it be named. If you pray, you can ask God about it once more, honestly, the way Paul did, and then listen for what might carry you if it stays. If you don't, simply hold it, and ask what has helped you live with it so far. The bell holds the time.
Unanswered prayer. A prayer that seems to get no, like Paul's thrice-asked thorn, answered instead with grace that is enough.
Your line: my grace is sufficient. Today, when your thorn presses, say the line to yourself once, and notice one thing that's still carrying you. Day one thousand three hundred eighty-nine.

howItsDone: Christians keep praying for healing and help for themselves and others, and when an answer doesn't come, some turn to Paul's thorn and Jesus's prayer in Gethsemane, praying for grace to carry what remains.

original.note: Greek: a thorn, or a sharp stake, the word Paul uses for his thorn in the flesh.

trapdoor: what you thought: an unanswered prayer means God wasn't listening.
what it means: Paul asked three times, the thorn stayed, and the answer was grace enough to live with it.
what a scholar hears: skolops can mean a thorn or a pointed stake, something more than a splinter. Paul never names it, and readers' guesses still differ.

notes: 'traveled from city to city starting churches' is a summary of Acts, not of the cited verses. Confirm.
Readers' guesses about the thorn (illness, eye trouble, an opponent, temptation) are presented as guesses; the eye-trouble reading leans on Galatians 4:13–15. Confirm.
Trapdoor: skolops as 'thorn' or 'pointed stake': lexical claim. Confirm.
'Christians sometimes say every prayer gets an answer, and sometimes the answer is no': a common saying, attributed to 'sometimes'. Confirm.
2 Corinthians 12:10 ('when I am weak, then am I strong') is saved for tomorrow.
